title: Hatch Warren Infant School: 14 July 2026
text:
Determination
Case reference: VAR2748
Admission authority: Hampshire County Council
School: Hatch Warren Infant School
Date of decision: 14 July 2026
Determination
In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by
Hampshire County Council for Hatch Warren Infant School in 2026/27.
I determine that the published admission number for the school in 2026/27 will be 60.
The referral
1. Hampshire County Council (the Local Authority (LA or HCC)) has referred to the
adjudicator a proposal for a variation to the admission arrangements of Hatch Warren Infant
School (HWIS or the School) in 2026/27 (the Arrangements).
2. The School is a community school for children aged 4 to 7 in Basingstoke,
Hampshire. It is a co-educational and non-selective infant school with no designated
religious character.
3. HWIS was judged to be ‘Good’ by Ofsted in all inspected areas at its last inspection
in June 2022.
4. The proposed variation is for the published admission number (PAN) of the School to
be reduced from 90 to 60 in 2026/27.
Jurisdiction and procedure
5. The referral was made to me in accordance with section 88E of the School
Standards and Framework Act 1998 (the Act) which deals with variations to determined

arrangements. Paragraphs 3.6 and 3.7 of the School Admissions Code (the Code) say (as
far as relevant here):
“3.6 Once admission arrangements have been determined for a particular school
year, they cannot be revised by the admission authority unless such revision is
necessary to give effect to a mandatory requirement of this Code, admissions law, a
determination of the Adjudicator or any misprint in the admission arrangements.
Admission authorities may propose other variations where they consider such
changes to be necessary in view of a major change in circumstances. Such
proposals must be referred to the Schools Adjudicator for approval, and the
appropriate bodies notified. Where the local authority is the admission authority for a
community or voluntary controlled school, it must consult the governing body of the
school before making any reference.
3.7 Admission authorities must notify the appropriate bodies of all variations”.
6. The arrangements were determined by the LA’s Executive Member for Education on
12 February 2025. The LA has provided me with confirmation that the appropriate bodies
have been notified, and I have seen confirmation that the School’s Governing Body has
been consulted on the proposed variation. I find that the appropriate procedures were
followed, and I am also satisfied that the proposed variation is within my jurisdiction.
7. In considering the variation request I have had regard to all relevant legislation, and
the Code.
8. The information I have considered in reaching my decision includes:
a. the referral from the LA dated 2 June 2026 and supporting documents;
b. the determined arrangements for 2026/27 and the proposed variation to those
arrangements;
c. responses received from the School and the LA in response to requests for
further information; and
d. information available on the websites of the LA, the School, the Department for
Education (DfE) (including ‘Get Information About Schools’ (GIAS) and ‘Financial
Benchmarking and Insights Tool’ (FBIT)) and Ofsted.
9. There is no formal consultation required for a variation and so parents and others do
not have the opportunity to express their views. Clearly, it is desirable that changes to
arrangements are made via the process of determination following consultation as the
consultation process allows those with an interest to express their views. It also allows for
objections to the adjudicator. None of this is afforded by the variation process.
2

10. I note here that the arrangements for 2027/28 have already been determined. This
means that the request to amend the arrangements for 2026/27 will be for that year only
and will not have the effect of forming the ‘baseline’ PAN for following years.
11. I have been asked to consider this request late in the academic year. I felt it
important that the decision on the PAN reduction be made swiftly, such that it can be
implemented in good time. I have not, therefore, undertaken an assessment of the
Arrangements as a whole under section 88I of the Act. The Admission Authority should not
take the fact that I have not raised any other matters about the Arrangements as an
endorsement of their compliance with the Code.
12. I wish to convey my thanks to the LA for its response to my request for further
information.
Consideration of proposed variation
13. Paragraph 3.6 of the Code (as above) requires that admission arrangements, once
determined, may only be revised, that is changed or varied, if there is a major change of
circumstance or certain other limited and specified circumstances. I will consider below
whether the variation requested is justified by the change in circumstances.
14. The LA told me that the reason for it seeking a variation for the School is:
“The Published Admission Number (PAN) for Hatch Warren Infant School for
2026/27 is 90. However, for the 2026 admissions round, the school received only 51
offers. As a result, and with the support of the Local Authority, the school is seeking
to reduce its PAN to 60 for Year R admissions in September 2026. This low number
of offers for September 2026 is expected to exacerbate the school’s worsening
financial position following a year of operating below capacity with currently only 77
pupils on roll in year R against a PAN of 90.”
15. The LA has a duty to make sure that there are sufficient places for the children in its
area. To fulfil this duty the LA assesses the likely future number of places to be needed and
plans to meet that need. The geographical area covered by the LA is divided up into
‘planning areas’ for this purpose. Each planning area is made up of a small group of
schools.
16. The School is one of nine schools for primary aged children in the LA’s ‘Basingstoke
Area E’ planning area (BAE or the planning area). There are five other schools in the
planning area that admit children to Reception (YR) are (in order of straight line distance (in
miles) from the postcode of the HWIS site taken from the DfE’s GIAS website): Manor Field
Infant School (0.41); St Mark's Church of England Primary School (0.46); Kempshott Infant
School (0.77); Chalk Ridge Primary School (0.91); and Hounsome Fields Primary School
(1.27). The remaining schools in the planning area are: Hatch Warren Junior School (0.04);
3

Manor Field Junior School (0.41); and Kempshott Junior School (0.75). As these three
schools admit to Year 3 and not YR, I will not consider them any further.
17. HWIS was graded ‘Good’ in all inspected areas in June 2022. Putting aside
Hounsome Fields Primary School (which has not yet been inspected as it only opened in
2025). none of the other schools admitting to YR in the BAE have been judged by Ofsted to
be below the ‘Expected Standard’ (if inspected post-November 2025) or ‘Good’ (in
individual inspection areas if inspected after September and before November 2025 or
overall if inspected prior to September 2025) either as an overall judgement or in individual
categories (depending on when it was inspected). has not been inspected by Ofsted. This
means that all places available in the BAE are in schools judged to be providing at least the
expected standard of education.
18. About this planning area, the LA told me that:
“Regarding the wider planning area, within Basingstoke - Area E, there are a total of
325 offers for September 2026 for Year R against a combined capacity of 390,
leaving a surplus of 65 places, equivalent to over 2 forms of entry. Across the
planning area, Chalk Ridge Primary School have received 27 offers against a PAN of
30, Hounsome Fields Primary School have received 30 offers against a PAN of 30,
Kempshott Infant School have received 77 offers against a PAN of 90, Manor Field
Infant School have received 50 offers against a PAN of 60 and St Mark's C Of E
Primary School have received 90 offers against a PAN of 90. This demonstrates that
there is capacity within the planning area should the PAN reduction be approved.”
19. If I do not approve the reduction in the PAN in 2026/27, that would leave a surplus of
65 places (16.6 per cent of the total PAN). If I approve the PAN at HWIS being reduced to
60 in 2026/27, this will have the effect of reducing the number of YR places for children in
the BAE to 360 for that academic year. This would leave a surplus of 35 places (9.7 per
cent of places).
20. The DfE document, “Basic need allocations 2025-26: Explanatory note on
methodology”, refers to the need for two per cent surplus capacity “to provide an operating
margin for local authorities … to support parental choice, pupil population movement, and
general manageability of the system”. I note that the proportion of vacant places in the
planning area will be considerably higher than two per cent and would continue to be if I
approve the proposed reduction in PAN.
21. Turning now to the School, I note the LA’s description of the class structure:
“The current class structure at Hatch Warren Infant School comprises three Year R
classes, three Year 1 classes, and three Year 2 classes, all operating below
capacity. This level of undersubscription is creating substantial challenges for the
school and placing severe financial pressure on its budget.”
4

22. I looked at the School’s financial position. This is because schools are funded, in
large part, on a per child basis. A reduction in the number of children admitted, therefore,
results in a reduction in income. Additionally, the provisions of the School Admissions
(Infant Class Size) (England) Regulations 2012 (the infant class size regulations) apply to
the School, and they require that infant classes (those where the majority of children will
reach the age of five, six or seven during the school year) must not contain more than 30
children with a single qualified teacher, except in specific exceptional circumstances.
23. I noted from the FBIT website that in the financial year 2024-25 (up to March 2025),
the School had an in-year deficit of -£112,144 and a revenue reserve deficit of -£125,295.
24. As the School is currently running a budget deficit, the Governing Body are expected
to work with the LA to work towards a balanced budget. The School's financial projections
are such that a reduction in the PAN for YR in 2026/27 will significantly help the financial
pressure the School is under. Hence the Governing Body requested that the LA make this
variation request to the adjudicator. The Governing Body and the LA are concerned that
continuing to staff and resource the School for a higher number of children (three classes of
30) than is currently projected to be admitted (less than two classes of 30) would cause
further financial difficulty at a time when the School is required to address its budget issues.
A PAN of 60 would allow for two classes of 30; this removes the cost of staffing and
resourcing a third class.
25. I note from the minutes of the Governing Body meeting on 5 May 2026 that there
was unanimous support for the PAN reduction as a means by which the school can
continue to address its financial issues.
26. In my view, the Governing Body at the School and the LA are working to address the
financial shortfall in the School’s budget. Reducing the PAN for the School for 2026/27 will
have no effect on parental preference in the normal admission round as offers have been
made and there are less admissions than there are places. The number of offers made will
remain fewer than the number of places with a reduced PAN. There will be nine places
available at the School for any in-year applicants and, as set out earlier, there are places
available in other schools admitting children into YR in the BAE. Aside from Hounsome
Fields Primary School, Ofsted have judged the education at all of those schools to be at the
same level or better than at HWIS; parents will, therefore, have a good choice of schools in
the local area.
27. The data provided by the LA demonstrated that it has a clear picture of recent /
projected demand in schools in the BAE. It appeared to me that the matter raised in respect
of the PAN at HWIS and the surplus places in the BAE in 2026/27 would have been
obvious in enough time for what has been requested to have been dealt with through the
consultation process prior to the determination of the Arrangements. I raised this concern
with the LA and its response was:
5

“There was no clear basis for a reduction in the school's PAN in Autumn 2024 when
any reduction to [the YR] intake [was] consulted upon. At the point when admission
arrangements for September 2026 were being considered, forecasts indicated that
there would be 74 [YR] pupils in 2026, rising to 79 [YR] pupils in 2027 (please see
the forecast below). Whilst these figures were below the school's PAN of 90, they did
not suggest a sustained reduction in demand that would justify reducing the PAN to
75 or 60. In particular, a reduction to 60 would only typically be considered where
forecasts indicated [YR] pupil numbers consistently at, or below that level, enabling
the school to maintain discrete year groups while operating sustainably.
In addition. when the 2026 admission arrangements were being consulted on in
autumn 2024, the school had exceeded its own [YR] forecast, with 90 pupils taking
up places against a forecast of 80. This demonstrated that actual pupil numbers
could vary and indicated that pupil numbers might continue to fluctuate. It should
also be noted that the impact of the new Hounsome Fields school, which opened in
September 2025, could not be fully assessed when admission arrangements for
September 2026 were being determined.
Although demand was forecast to be below the school's PAN of 90, the reductions
projected at that time were not sufficiently significant or sustained to justify
consultation on a lower PAN. Furthermore, the available evidence did not indicate
that the school would be able to reduce the number of classes.”
28. I consider the LA’s reasons for not consulting for a reduction in PAN, prior to the
determination of the Arrangements, to be understandable. Should any future reductions in
PAN be required, it is preferable that they are undertaken through the consultation process
wherever possible.
29. Taking all of the above into account, I agree to the proposed reduction in the PAN
from 90 to 60 in 2026/27.
30. I note here that reducing the PAN does not reduce the overall capacity of the School
unless accommodation is being removed from the premises. It is not being suggested that
accommodation is being removed and so the physical capacity of the School remains the
same. Reducing the PAN will not change that. What this means is that should there be a
need for the PAN of the School to be increased and / or for more children to be admitted
from 2026/27 than is currently expected, there remains the capacity in the building for the
LA to do so.
Determination
31. In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by Hampshire
County Council for Hatch Warren Infant School in 2026/27.
6

32. I determine that the published admission number for the school in 2026/27 will be 60.
Dated: 14 July 2026
Signed:
Schools adjudicator: Dr Robert Cawley

title: East Meon Church of England Controlled Primary School: 14 July 2026
text:
Determination
Case reference: VAR2766
Admission Authority: Hampshire County Council for East Meon Church
of England Controlled Primary School
Date of decision: 14 July 2026
Determination
In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by
Hampshire County Council for East Meon Church of England Controlled Primary
School, for 2026.
I determine that for admission in 2026 the published admission number will be five.
The referral
1. Hampshire County Council (the Local Authority or LA) has referred to the adjudicator
a proposal for a variation to the admission arrangements for East Meon Church of England
Controlled Primary School (the School or EMPS) for 2026 (the Arrangements).
2. EMPS is a voluntary controlled primary school for children aged four to eleven years.
It sits within the village of East Meon, west of Petersfield in Hampshire, and is a co-
educational, non-selective school. EMPS has a Church of England religious character, and
the faith body for the School is the Diocese of Portsmouth (the Diocese).
3. The Admission Authority for the School is the Local Authority. As the LA is the
Admission Authority, both terms are used throughout this determination.
4. Parties to the request are the LA, the School and the Diocese.
5. The proposed variation is that the published admission number (PAN), which applies
to the Reception Year (Year R), be reduced from 13 to five. I say more about the current
PAN below.

Jurisdiction and procedure
6. Section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998 (the Act) makes
provision for variations to determined arrangements. Paragraphs 3.6 and 3.7 of the School
Admissions Code (the Code) say (insofar as is relevant here):
“3.6 Once admission arrangements have been determined for a particular school year,
they cannot be revised by the admission authority unless such revision is necessary to
give effect to a mandatory requirement of this Code, admissions law, a determination
of the Adjudicator or any misprint in the admission arrangements. Admission
authorities may propose other variations where they consider such changes to be
necessary in view of a major change in circumstances. Such proposals must be
referred to the Schools Adjudicator for approval, and the appropriate bodies notified.
Where the local authority is the admission authority for a community or voluntary
controlled school, it must consult the governing body of the school before making any
reference.
3.7 Admission authorities must notify the appropriate bodies of all variations”.
7. The Arrangements were determined by the Admission Authority on 12 February
2025. The Admission Authority has provided me with confirmation that the appropriate
bodies have been notified of the proposed variation in line with the Code. I find that the
appropriate procedures were followed, and I am satisfied that the proposed variation is
within my jurisdiction.
8. In the interests of dealing speedily with this request for a variation, I have not
considered other aspects of the Arrangements. Therefore, nothing in this determination
should be taken as indicating that other aspects of the Arrangements do or do not conform
with the requirements relating to admissions.
9. In considering the variation request I have had regard to all relevant legislation and
the Code.
10. The information I have considered in reaching my decision includes:
• the referral from the Admission Authority dated 18 June 2026 and supporting
documents;
• the determined Arrangements for 2026 and the proposed variation to those
Arrangements;
• responses from the LA, the School and the Diocese to my requests for further
information;
• maps, including Google Maps and those showing the location of the School;
• information available on the government website ‘Get Information About Schools’
(GIAS); and
2

• information available on the website of the LA, including the admission
arrangements for EMPS for 2027.
11. There is no formal consultation required for a variation and so parents and others do
not have the opportunity to express their views. Clearly it is desirable that changes to
arrangements are made via the process of determination following consultation as the
consultation process allows those with an interest to express their views. It also allows for
objections to the adjudicator. None of this is afforded by the variation process.
12. I note here that the Arrangements for 2027 have been determined, and a PAN of 15
has been set. Consequently, if I agree to the Admission Authority’s request to vary the
Arrangements for 2026 by reducing the PAN as proposed, it will be for that year only and
will not have a bearing on subsequent years.
Consideration of proposed variation
13. Paragraph 3.6 of the Code (as above) requires that admission arrangements, once
determined, may only be revised, that is changed or varied, if there is a major change of
circumstance or certain other limited and specified circumstances. I will consider below
whether the proposed variation is justified by the change in circumstances.
14. The Admission Authority has proposed that the PAN of the School is reduced from 13
to five for entry to Year R in September 2026. The proposal has the support of the School
and of the Diocese. The referral gave the reason for seeking a variation as follows:
“This application to the Office of the Schools Adjudicator (OSA) seeks approval to
reduce the Published Admission Number (PAN) for East Meon CE Primary from 13
to 5 for September 2026. This reduction is necessary to align the PAN with actual
and projected pupil numbers and to secure the school’s ongoing financial and
organisational viability.
For September 2026, East Meon CE Primary received just 5 offers against a PAN of
13. . . Due to offers being below the PAN, the school is no longer able to
viably operate four classes, and maintaining the current PAN would place significant
and ongoing financial pressure on the school. Implementing the proposed PAN
reduction would enable the school to move to three classes, creating a financially
sustainable structure that more accurately reflects the demand for places.”
15. I pause to consider the current PAN of the School. The referral states, as above, that
the PAN is 13; that is also the figure published in the Arrangements. However, data
accompanying the referral uses a PAN of 15. Assuming there was a typographical error in
the data, I sought clarification from the LA, which stated:
“The PAN of 15 for 2026 is not a typographical error. While increases in PAN are
typically referenced within the annual admissions consultation, the School
Admissions Code does not require such increases to be formally consulted upon. In
this instance, the request to increase the PAN was received after the consultation
3

process had already commenced. Therefore, revised PAN of 15 for 2026 onwards
was agreed.”
16. The LA is correct that increases to PAN may be made without consultation. However,
it is not clear to me whether a PAN of 15 was “agreed”, as the LA has stated, as part of
determining the Arrangements or following their determination.
17. If a PAN of 15 was determined, then the Arrangements should show that figure; they
do not do so. If the LA determined a PAN of 13 and subsequently varied it to 15, as
provided for by Paragraph 3.6 of the Code which allows increases to PAN without referral to
the adjudicator, then the Arrangements should have been revised accordingly. The
Arrangements have not been revised, and I have seen no evidence that such a variation
was agreed by the Admission Authority. Consequently, I consider the PAN to be 13. In the
interest of completeness, I note that paragraph 1.4 of the Code allows for admissions above
the level of the PAN; such admissions do not constitute an increase to the PAN, as stated
in paragraph 1.5 of the Code.
18. I have given careful consideration to the latest available data in order to form a view
about the sufficiency of school places in the local area if the PAN of the School is reduced
from 13 to five. I have also considered the demand for places at the School, the potential
effect of the proposed PAN reduction on meeting parental preference, and whether the
proposed reduction is justified taking into account all relevant circumstances.
19. The Local Authority has a duty to make sure that there are sufficient places for the
children in its area. It uses planning areas, which are geographical areas each containing a
number of schools, for this purpose. In the planning area to which the School belongs, there
are eight schools (including the School) which admit pupils to Year R. Table 1, below,
shows: the sum of the PANs at those schools; and the number of children admitted in each
of 2023, 2024 and 2025. Table 1 also shows the number of children offered a place for
2026 (as of 4 June) and demonstrates the effect on surplus places of reducing the PAN of
the School as has been proposed.

20. The Department for Education document, “Basic need allocations 2026-27 and 2027-
28: Explanatory note on methodology”, refers to the need for two per cent surplus capacity
“to provide an operating margin for local authorities. This helps to support parental choice,
pupil population movement, and general manageability of the system”. From the data in
table 1, I am satisfied that if the PAN of the School were to be reduced to five for 2026,
there would be sufficient places available in the planning area for any children who might be
seeking a Year R place.
21. I will now consider the demand for places at the School. Table 2 shows the number of
first preference applications received, and the number of children admitted in each of 2024
and 2025. It also shows the number of offers made for 2026, as of 4 June.

22. The data in table 2 show a fall in the number of first preference applications for 2026.
The data also show that all the children whose parents wanted their child to be admitted to
EMPS in September have been offered a place; the number of offers is significantly below
the PAN. The LA has told me that the five offers made for 2026 comprise four made on
National Offer Day and one made subsequently, I assume to a late applicant.
5

23. The proposed variation would have no effect on parental preference in respect of
applications received as part of the normal admissions process for September 2026.
However, if the proposed variation is approved, then no vacant places will remain at the
School. I cannot, therefore, rule out the possibility that some parents may be disappointed:
namely, any more who may apply late, and parents who seek a place during the course of
the 2026/27 school year.
24. As set out earlier, there are Year R places available within the planning area for 2026.
As of 4 June, three of the other seven schools in that area had vacant spaces. However,
the location of EMPS is, as recorded on GIAS, “smaller rural”. GIAS shows that there are
only two other schools which admit pupils to Year R within three miles of the School, and
that the closest of these is approximately 2.7 miles distant, measured as a straight line. If,
say, a family with a child of Year R age moves into East Meon village during the 2026 / 27
school year they will, if no places remain at EMPS, be obliged to travel some distance to the
next nearest school at which a place is available.
25. The School is affected by the provisions of the School Admissions (Infant Class Size)
(England) Regulations 2012 which require that infant classes (those where the majority of
children will reach the age of five, six or seven during the school year) must not contain
more than 30 pupils with a single qualified schoolteacher except in specific exceptional
circumstances. The infant class size regulations apply to Year R, Year 1 and Year 2.
Children at the School are currently organised into one, single age class for Year R. The
other year groups are organised into mixed-age classes, giving a total of four classes in the
School. If the variation was agreed then all the children could be taught in mixed age
groups, with children in Year R, Year 1 and Year 2 in one class of 30 pupils. This would
result in three total classes with associated financial savings.
26. If the PAN remained at 13 and, say, one further late applicant was admitted to the
School, there would be 31 total children in Year R, Year 1 and Year 2. Those children could
not be taught by a single teacher without breaching the Infant Class Size Regulations and
would need to be taught in two small classes, which is unlikely to be financially viable. As
the PAN would apply to Year R for the entirety of the 2026/27 academic year, the School
would also be required to admit any child whose parents requested a Year R place, until 13
children had been admitted. Even if the number of children admitted on the first day of term
in September 2026 was 5 or fewer and the School was able to operate its planned
organisation of three total classes, any in-year admissions would be likely to necessitate a
reorganisation midway through the year. If, however, the proposed variation was agreed,
the School would be able to plan with certainty.
27. This situation is recognised by the School, which told me:
“As a result of a low existing intake for the 2026 Year R class of only 5 pupils, to
remain financially viable the School will have to reduce the number of its classes
from 4 to 3, resulting in a new combined Years R, 1 and 2 class from September
2026. . .
6

As a result, if the application to vary the 2026 Year R PAN to 5 is not agreed then if
the School were to receive any further pupil intake for the 2026 Year R, the result
could be the School having to open a new class and employ another teacher for a
potentially low level of additional Year R intake. This would place a financial burden
on the School which it cannot afford based on its current pupil numbers; leading to a
fiscal deficit for the School.”
28. The LA provided helpful financial information which it summarised as follows:
“A financial analysis of the school shows that under the original forecast based on a
PAN of 13 the school’s position deteriorates rapidly moving from a surplus of
£45,730 in 2025/26 to a substantial deficit on -£152,416 by 2027/28, reflecting the
cost of running four classes driving increasingly large in-year deficits each year. In
contrast, the revised forecast based on a PAN of 5 significantly slows this decline.
Although still moving into deficit by 2027/28, the cumulative shortfall is much smaller
at -£42,003. The reduction in PAN therefore improves the overall financial position by
approximately £110,000 over the three-year period and delays the onset of a
negative financial position, maintaining a surplus into 2026/27 rather than falling into
deficit earlier. Therefore, the lower PAN and reduction in classes reduces financial
pressure and improves the school’s sustainability.”
29. I have weighed this case carefully. The proposed variation would result in there
being no vacant Year R places at the School. It is possible that families may consequently
be refused admission during the 2026 / 27 school year, and experience difficulties with
travel to alternative schools due to the rurality of the area as I have described above.
However, the size of the School, and the position of its finances, are such that if the PAN is
not reduced then its sustainability may be affected. On balance, I consider that it is
reasonable to conclude that the proposed variation is justified by the circumstances. I
approve the proposed variation to reduce the PAN for 2026 from 13 to five.
30. I note here that reducing the PAN does not reduce the overall capacity of the School
unless accommodation is being removed from the premises. It is not being suggested that
accommodation is being removed and so the physical capacity of the School remains the
same. Reducing the PAN will not change that. What this means is that should there be a
need for the School to admit more children than it currently expects to, there remains the
capacity in the building for it to do so.
31. For the avoidance of doubt, I note the following which was included in a letter sent to
me by the School:
“Please do however note that we are only seeking to reduce the PAN for the 2026
Year R intake (and would like to retain a PAN of 13 for the 2027 Year R intake and
thereafter).”
32. The published, determined arrangements for 2027 state a PAN of 15. As I have said,
my determination has no bearing on that year. Consequently, the PAN of the School for
7

2027 is 15, and may not be reduced unless a proposal for a variation is agreed by the
adjudicator.
Determination
33. In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by Hampshire
County Council for East Meon Church of England Controlled Primary School, for 2026.
34. I determine that for admission in 2026 the published admission number will be five.

title: Silsoe Church of England Voluntary Controlled Lower School: 14 July 2026
text:
Determination
Case reference: VAR2753
Admission Authority: Central Bedfordshire Council for Silsoe Church of
England Voluntary Controlled Lower School
Date of decision: 14 July 2026
Determination
In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
do not approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by
Central Bedfordshire Council for Silsoe Church of England Voluntary Controlled
Lower School for 2026/27.
The published admission number for admissions to the Reception Year in 2026/27
shall remain at 60.
The referral
1. Central Bedfordshire Council (the Admission Authority; the Local Authority) has
referred to the adjudicator a proposal for a variation to the admission arrangements (the
Arrangements) for Silsoe Church of England Voluntary Controlled Lower School (the
School) for 2026/27.
2. The School is a voluntary controlled school for children aged four to nine years in the
village of Silsoe, Bedfordshire. It is a co-educational school with a Church of England
religious character. The Diocese of St Albans (the Diocese) is the religious authority for the
School.
3. The proposed variation is that the published admission number (PAN) of the School,
which applies to admissions to the Reception Year (Year R), be reduced from 60, as
determined, to 30 for 2026/27.

Jurisdiction and procedure
4. Section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998 (the Act) makes
provision for variations to determined arrangements. Paragraphs 3.6 and 3.7 of the School
Admissions Code (the Code) say (insofar as is relevant here):
“3.6 Once admission arrangements have been determined for a particular school year,
they cannot be revised by the admission authority unless such revision is necessary to
give effect to a mandatory requirement of this Code, admissions law, a determination
of the Adjudicator or any misprint in the admission arrangements. Admission
authorities may propose other variations where they consider such changes to be
necessary in view of a major change in circumstances. Such proposals must be
referred to the Schools Adjudicator for approval, and the appropriate bodies notified.
Where the local authority is the admission authority for a community or voluntary
controlled school, it must consult the governing body of the school before making any
reference.
3.7 Admission authorities must notify the appropriate bodies of all variations”.
5. The Arrangements were determined by the Local Authority on 12 February 2025.
6. The Local Authority has provided me with confirmation that the appropriate bodies
have been notified of the proposed variation in line with the Code, and that the governing
body of the School has been consulted on the proposed variation. I find that the appropriate
procedures were followed, and I am satisfied that the proposed variation is within my
jurisdiction.
7. In considering the variation request, I have had regard to all relevant legislation and
the Code.
8. The information I have considered in reaching my decision includes:
• the referral from the Local Authority dated 9 June 2026 and supporting
documents;
• the determined Arrangements and the proposed variation to those Arrangements;
• responses from the Local Authority, the Diocese, and the governing body of the
School to my requests for further information;
• maps, including Google Maps and those showing the location of the School; and
• information available on the websites of .gov.uk. (including the ‘Get Information
About Schools’ (GIAS) and ‘Financial Benchmarking and Insights Tool’ (FBIT)
websites), the Local Authority, and the School.
2

9. There is no formal consultation required for a variation and so parents and others do
not have the opportunity to express their views. Clearly it is desirable that changes to
arrangements are made via the process of determination following consultation as the
consultation process allows those with an interest to express their views. It also allows for
objections to the adjudicator. None of this is afforded by the variation process.
10. I note here that the Arrangements for 2027/28 have been determined, and the PAN is
set at 60. This means that if I agree to the Admission Authority’s request to vary the
Arrangements for 2026/27 by reducing the PAN as proposed, it will be for that year only
and will not have a bearing on subsequent years.
11. In the interest of dealing speedily with this and other requests for variations for
schools, I have not considered other aspects of the Arrangements. Therefore, nothing in
this determination should be taken as indicating that other aspects of the Arrangements do
or do not conform with the requirements relating to admissions.
Consideration of proposed variation
12. Paragraph 3.6 of the Code (as above) requires that admission arrangements, once
determined, may only be revised, that is changed or varied, if there is a major change of
circumstance or certain other limited and specified circumstances. I will consider below
whether the proposed variation is justified by the change in circumstances.
13. The Local Authority has proposed that the PAN of the School be reduced from 60 to
30 for admissions in 2026/27. The proposed variation has the support of the Diocese and
the School’s governing body.
14. The Local Authority told me the following reason for it seeking a variation to the PAN
for the School:
“The school currently has 31 pupils allocated for the new Reception year group in
September 2026. The Governing Body has asked the Council as its admission
authority to reduce the published admissions number from 60 to 30 for this September
2026 due to the low pupil numbers.
The pupil numbers for the school for the new intake are greatly reduced compared to
previous years. Operating two classes will cause the school financial hardship (the
school already has a deficit budget,) as the pupil AWPU [Aged Weighted Pupil Unit]
for 31 pupils currently allocated will not cover the costs of two teachers. The school
are hoping to operate one class if pupil numbers decrease to 30 by September. The
school has decided not to recruit to a maternity leave cover post but will use supply
teacher if still at 31 pupils or above.”
15. I have considered the latest available data to form a view about the sufficiency of
school places in the local area if the PAN of the School is reduced from 60 to 30 in 2026/27.
I have also considered the demand for places at the School, the reasons given for the
change in demand, the potential effect of the proposed PAN reduction on parental
3

preference, and whether the proposed reduction is justified taking into account all relevant
circumstances.
16. The Local Authority has a duty to ensure that there are sufficient places for the
children in its area. To fulfil this duty, the Local Authority assesses the likely future number
of places to be needed and plans to meet that need. The Local Authority uses planning
areas, which are geographical areas and the schools within those areas, for this purpose.
The School is located in ‘Harlington Cluster’ (the planning area), and I have considered the
data that the Local Authority has provided for that area.
17. Along with the School there are four other schools in the planning area for which the
usual year of entry is Year R. The combined PAN of the planning area is 195 for Year R
entry for September 2026, and the latest number of children offered a place is 149.
18. Table 1 below shows the latest data provided by the Local Authority in relation to
admissions to Year R in September 2026. All of those other lower schools (as the schools
for children aged four to nine years are referred to) are more than two miles away (by
walking distance, or by car) from the School. The two closest schools within the planning
area are fully subscribed and do not have any vacant places for Year R entry in September
2026.

19. The DfE document, ‘Basic need allocations 2026-27 and 2027-28: Explanatory note
on methodology’, refers to the need for two per cent surplus capacity to “to provide an
operating margin for local authorities. This helps to support parental choice, pupil
population movement, and general manageability of the system.” Although a reduction of
the School’s Year R places by 30 places will render a surplus of 18 vacant places for the
entire planning area (about 10 per cent), these vacancies within the wide ‘planning area’
are not easily accessible to those living near to the School.
20. Most parents seeking a Year R place for their child for admissions in the 2026/27
would have been offered a place on National Offer Day in April. That said, if a family were
to make a late or in-year application for a Year R place at the School, the School may still
4

provide a place now with its many vacancies. The proposed PAN reduction by 30 places
will, in effect, make the School ‘oversubscribed’ and remove entirely an operating margin for
the Local Authority in relation to the provision of Year R places for the local area in which
the School is located.
21. It is therefore not possible to say that, if the PAN of the School were to be reduced to
30 for 2026/27, there would be sufficient places for any parents living close to the School
and seeking a Year R place for their child for 2026/27, including those who are to make late
or in-year admissions.
22. I turn now to the demand for places at the School. An additional place has been
allocated to an applicant since this referral was submitted to the adjudicator on 9 June
2026. There are 32 applicants who are now allocated Year R places at the School for
September 2026. In its response dated 30 June 2026 to my request for further information,
the School stated:
“We currently have 32 pupils in Reception for September 2026/2027. However, one
family is actively seeking an alternative setting so that their Reception-aged child can
attend the same school as their siblings. In addition, another pupil who is moving into
the area has requested a Reception place.”
23. The Local Authority stated in its reply of 3 July 2026:
“We still have 32 children for a place at Silsoe CofE VC Lower School for Year R in
September 2026 and are unaware at present of any declines or changes of
preferences to process which may change this.”
24. The Admission Authority is required to admit all these 32 children being in September
2026. This suggests that it is likely that the School will admit more than 30 pupils for Year R
in September 2026, and that there may be a small demand for late or in-year applications. If
any parents were unsuccessful in securing a place for their child at the School due to the
proposed PAN reduction, their alternative would be seeking a place at another school which
is, likely and undesirably, some miles away.
25. However small the possibility might be, there could be some frustration of parental
preference in relation to late or in-year applicants seeking to secure a Year R place at the
School, if the variation were to be agreed for 2026/27.
26. I will now consider the impact on the School of my approving, or not approving, the
proposed variation.
27. The School is one affected by the provisions of the School Admissions (Infant Class
Sizes) (England) Regulations 2012 (the Infant Class Sizes Regulations) which require that
infant classes (those where the majority of children will reach the age of five, six or seven
during the school year) must not contain more than 30 pupils with a single qualified teacher
except in specific exceptional circumstances (paragraph 2.16 of the Code). The Infant Class
Sizes Regulations apply to Year R, Year 1, and Year 2.
5

28. The School acknowledged that, in order to meet the statutory requirement under the
Infant Class Sizes Regulations, it will organise all Year R pupils into two classes in 2026/27
if the actual admissions are over 30. An alternative is mixed aged classes which the School
does not wish to consider for the reasons given below. It would also have two classes each
for year groups from Year 1 to Year 4.
29. As schools are largely funded on the number of pupils on roll and the most
expensive element of a school budget is staff, it is generally considered financially efficient
to have infant classes that have 30 pupils or close to, but below, 30 pupils. If a school has
classes that are many fewer than 30 (as in the case of the School), then this can mean that
the income from the number of pupils is less than the costs of providing a class. If this
happens over several classes, a school can have severe financial challenges.
30. It is therefore understandable why both the Local Authority and the School, supported
by the Diocese, are keen to pursue the PAN reduction for 2026/27. However, I can only
determine the matters now on the assumption that there has so far been no clear indication
if the number of Year R pupils being admitted to the School will be dropped to 30 or below
in September or some point in the future. Whether or not the variation is approved, an
admission authority must not withdraw an offer unless an exception under paragraph 2.13
of the Code applies.
31. The FBIT website shows that for the financial year ending March 2025, the School
had an in-year surplus of about £32,000, and a revenue reserve of £80,000. Both the Local
Authority and the School have shown me budgetary information to demonstrate that
maintaining 10 classes (including two Year R classes with pupils many fewer than 30) is
financially unsustainable for the School.
32. In response to my request for further information, the School stated:
“Governors are deeply concerned about the impact on the school's financial
sustainability should the variation not be approved. Based on current and projected
pupil numbers, maintaining a PAN of 60 would require the school to operate two
Reception classes for a cohort of approximately 30 pupils. This would result in an
inefficient use of resources and place an unsustainable burden on the school's
budget, significantly increasing the existing deficit.
The school is already implementing a workforce restructure in response to falling
pupil numbers and the associated reduction in funding. Governors have carefully
considered alternative options but do not believe there is any realistic or sustainable
means of addressing the financial pressures if the PAN remains at 60. In their view,
approval of the requested variation is essential to safeguard the school's long-term
financial viability.
The Governing Body has also considered the educational implications of maintaining
a higher PAN. Governors do not consider the introduction of mixed-age classes to be
an appropriate or sustainable solution. Parents have chosen the school with the
expectation that children will be taught in single year-group classes. A move to
6

mixed-age classes could adversely affect the school's attractiveness to prospective
families, increasing the risk of further declining admissions and a consequential
reduction in funding, thereby compounding the school's financial challenges.
Governors are committed to ensuring that pupils receive the highest quality
education. They believe that a single Reception class provides the most effective
environment for delivering the Early Years Foundation Stage curriculum, enabling
staff to focus on the specific developmental and learning needs of Reception-aged
children. Maintaining a dedicated Reception class supports high-quality teaching,
curriculum delivery and outcomes for pupils.
If the requested variation is approved, the school will be able to align its staffing
structure with projected pupil numbers, use its resources more efficiently and
continue to provide a high-quality educational experience within a financially
sustainable model.
If the variation is not approved, governors believe the school will face avoidable and
significant financial pressures, with an increased risk to its long-term sustainability.”
33. I have considered the competing needs of providing the school places that parents
want for their children and the financial viability of the School. I am sympathetic to the
financial and other consequential challenges brought to the School by the lower-than-
expected number of Year R pupils.
34. The Local Authority noted in its reply to my request for further information:
“Our pupil forecasts take into account the births in the area and trends and although
we have begun conversations with the school about the future published admissions
number, these conversations commenced after the consultation window for 2027/28.
We are therefore looking to lower the PAN for this academic year only at present. We
will review admissions for 2027 next April once offers have been made and we are
now considering consulting on a PAN of 30 for 2028.”
35. The Diocese’s view is as follows:
“The Diocesan Board of Education fully supports the proposed reduction of the PAN
from 60 to 30, because of the financial difficulties that would result if the school had to
open a second Reception class in September for only one or two pupils. It is
unfortunate that there was a 31st allocation to the school before the variation
application could be submitted, but the hope is that numbers in Reception will shortly
return to 30, which would allow for the school to operate only a single Reception class,
within the infant class size limit.”
36. Having considered all the matters above, my reasoning can be summarised as
follows:
• Even if the proposed variation is approved, the School would still be required to
admit all the 32 children given offers for entry to Year R in September 2026.
7

Unless any of them changed their plan resulting in the School having 30 Year R
pupils or fewer on roll, or unless one of the exceptions about ‘excepted pupils’
referred to in paragraph 2.16 of the Code applies, the School would unavoidably
provide for more than one Year R class (or employ more than one qualified
teacher) anyway. In other words, the variation would not change the fact that the
School is to plan now for the number of classes and teachers on the assumption
of having more than 30 pupils for Year R for September 2026 and the rest of the
school year. This variation, if approved now, would not make a material difference
in terms of outcome unless the number of Year R pupils for September 2026
would be dropped to 30 or below, but there is no certainty at this point in time that
this is or would be the case. In addition, there is a possibility that a few children
who might otherwise be admitted through late or in-year applications and whose
parents in such circumstances have expressed a preference for a Year R place at
the School will have that preference denied and might need to travel some
distance to find an alternative.
• If the proposed variation is not approved, the School would be obliged to offer a
Year R place up to the existing PAN of 60 for any applicant in 2026/27. This will
provide an operating margin for the Local Authority, and helps to support parental
choice and pupil population movement. I acknowledge that the School would
undertake measures to economise on its resources, and that it wishes to secure
its level of staffing and budget position in 2026/27 and beyond. It remains open to
the Local Authority to request a lower PAN if the situation were to change for
2026/27 at any point in the school year. The Local Authority may also consider
applying for a variation to the PAN for 2027/28 if the forecast data support such a
request, and parents would be able to apply for places for 2027/28 in the
knowledge of the reduced PAN for the School (if approved) and make their
decisions accordingly. Otherwise, if a fresh referral comes after National Offer
Day in April 2027, the School would hopefully still have time to make any
necessary change to its staffing and class organisation to accommodate the
allocated pupils for September 2027. Furthermore, the Local Authority would, by
then, have been able to consult on a PAN reduction for 2028/29 following the
normal procedures for making changes to admission arrangements under
paragraphs 1.45 to 1.48 of the Code (see paragraph 9 above). I stress that my
determination here has no bearing on any process of consultation, or on the PAN
that is to be determined by the Local Authority for the School for 2028/29.
37. Taking everything into consideration, I find on balance that the variation is not
justified by the circumstances and so I do not approve it. The PAN of the School for
2026/27 remains at 60 as the Local Authority determined in February 2025.
8

Determination
38. In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
do not approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by
Central Bedfordshire Council for Silsoe Church of England Voluntary Controlled Lower
School for 2026/27.
39. The published admission number for admissions to the Reception Year in 2026/27
shall remain at 60.

title: Broadstone Hall Primary School: 14 July 2026
text:
Determination
Case reference: VAR2760
Admission Authority: Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council for
Broadstone Hall Primary School
Date of decision: 14 July 2026
Determination
In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by
Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council for Broadstone Hall Primary School for
2027/28.
I determine that for admission in 2027/28 the published admission number will be 60.
The referral
1. Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council is the admission authority for Broadstone
Hall Primary School (the School) and has referred to the adjudicator a proposal for a
variation to the admission arrangements for the School for 2027/28 (the arrangements).
2. The School is a community school for children aged three to eleven years. Stockport
Metropolitan Borough Council is also the local authority for the area in which the School is
located and I shall refer to it as the local authority. The School is in an urban area with eight
other schools which admit children to reception year within one mile and around 90 within
three miles.
3. The proposed variation is that the published admission number (PAN) for the School
is reduced from 75 to 60 for admissions in 2027/28; a reduction of 15 places. The year of
entry is reception year and this is the year group to which the PAN applies.
Jurisdiction and procedure
4. Section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998 (the Act) makes
provision for variations to determined arrangements. Paragraphs 3.6 and 3.7 of the School
Admissions Code (the Code) say (insofar as is relevant here):

“3.6 Once admission arrangements have been determined for a particular school year,
they cannot be revised by the admission authority unless such revision is necessary to
give effect to a mandatory requirement of this Code, admissions law, a determination
of the Adjudicator or any misprint in the admission arrangements. Admission
authorities may propose other variations where they consider such changes to be
necessary in view of a major change in circumstances. Such proposals must be
referred to the Schools Adjudicator for approval, and the appropriate bodies notified.
Where the local authority is the admission authority for a community or voluntary
controlled school, it must consult the governing body of the school before making any
reference.
3.7 Admission authorities must notify the appropriate bodies of all variations”.
5. The arrangements were determined by the local authority on 10 February 2026. The
local authority has provided me with confirmation that the appropriate bodies have been
notified of the proposed variation in line with the Code and confirmation that the governing
body of the School has been consulted on the proposed variation and supports it.
6. I find that the appropriate procedures were followed, and I am satisfied that the
proposed variation is within my jurisdiction.
7. In the interest of dealing speedily with this and other cases, I have not considered
other aspects of the arrangements. Therefore, nothing in this determination should be taken
as indicating that other aspects of the arrangements do or do not conform with the
requirements relating to admissions.
8. In considering the variation request, I have had regard to all relevant legislation and
the Code.
9. The information I have considered in reaching my decision includes:
a) the referral from the local authority dated 16 June 2026;
b) the determined arrangements for 2027/28 and the proposed variation to those
arrangements;
c) responses from the School to my requests for further information;
d) maps showing the location of the School; and
e) information available on government websites including:
o ‘Get Information About Schools’ (GIAS);
o Ofsted;
o ‘Financial Benchmarking and Insights Tool’ (FBIT); and
o ‘Find and compare schools and colleges in England’ (the DfE website);
f) the websites for the local authority and the School.
2

10. There is no formal consultation required for a variation and so parents and others do
not have the opportunity to express their views. Clearly it is desirable that changes to
arrangements are made via the process of determination following consultation as the
consultation process allows those with an interest to express their views. It also allows for
objections to the adjudicator. None of this is afforded by the variation process.
11. The arrangements for 2028/29 have not yet been determined. This means that if I
decide to approve the proposed variation to the arrangements for 2027/28 as proposed, it
will have the effect of forming the ‘baseline’ for subsequent years. I note that the local
authority intends to consult on setting the PAN at 60 for 2028/29.
Consideration of proposed variation
12. Paragraph 3.6 of the Code (as above) requires that admission arrangements, once
determined, may only be revised, that is changed or varied, if there is a major change of
circumstance or certain other limited and specified circumstances. I will consider below
whether the proposed variation is justified by the change in circumstances.
13. The local authority told me that the reason for it seeking a variation for the School is
that the number of children needing a place in reception year is falling across the area and
at the School. Schools are funded largely by the number of pupils and the greatest cost is
staffing. This means that if a School has a number of small classes, it is unlikely to receive
sufficient funding to meet the costs. Most primary schools seek to have close to 30 pupils to
a class in order to be financially efficient.
14. The School is one subject to the School Admissions (Infant Class Sizes) (England)
Regulations 2012 (the Infant Class Size Regulations) which require that infant classes
(those where the majority of children will reach the age of five, six or seven during the
school year) must not contain more than 30 pupils with a single qualified school teacher
except in specific exceptional circumstances. The Infant Class Size Regulations apply to
reception year, year 1 and year 2.
15. The local authority and the School are concerned that the combination of falling
demand for the School and the requirements of the Infant Class Size Regulations means
that the School will accrue a financial deficit if the PAN is not reduced. I will first consider
the applications and admissions overall including whether there would be sufficient school
places in the area if I were to agree the variation. I will then consider demand for places at
the School and the reasons for the variation request.
16. The local authority has a duty to ensure that there are sufficient school places for the
children in its area. To fulfil this duty the local authority assesses the likely future number of
places to be needed and plans to meet that need. The local authority uses planning areas,
which are geographical areas and the schools within those areas, for this purpose. The
School is in a planning area of eight schools, including the School, which admit children to
reception year.
3

17. Parents can apply for admission for their children wherever they wish and will make
their decisions based on their circumstances and will consider factors such as convenience,
family connections and reputation. Parents will take no account of planning areas when
applying for a school place.

18. When applying for a school place, parents in the local authority’s area are able to
express up to six preferences. A first preference is the school to which a parent would most
like their child to be admitted. Table 1 shows that demand has reduced in the planning area
from 400 children offered places for 2024/25 to 347 offered places for 2026/27. The number

vacant places forecast for 2027 and I am assured that if the PAN were reduced to 60 that
there would be sufficient places to meet demand for 2027/28. The number of vacancies
forecast for 2028/29 is similar to 2027/28 so I am not concerned that setting the baseline
would lead to a lack of places for 2028/29.
19. I will now consider demand for the School, parental preference and the reasons for

20. I note that the local authority said,
“it is important to consider the nuances of parental preference and the actual number
of children offered places in previous years. For the September 2026 intake, the
forecast was 65, yet only 63 pupils were offered places on National Offer Day and
this has since dropped to 62 pupils. Similarly, for the 2025 intake, the forecast was
73, and 70 pupils started on the first day of the academic year.”
21. FBIT recorded that at the end of the financial year April 2024 to March 2025, the in-
year balance was £64,247 and the reserves were £97,325. I asked the School to provide
further information about its finances and the planned class organisation taking into account
whether I agreed the variation or not.
22. The School told me that for the end of the 2025 – 2026 financial year, the in-year
balance was £56,453 and the revenue reserve was £153,778. Therefore the financial
situation for the School improved in the last financial year. However, the School forecasts
for 2027 – 2028, the School would have a revenue reserve deficit of £139,466 if the
variation is not agreed. Clearly all forecast figures are subject to a variety of factors but give
an indication of possible outcomes. I note that once a school is in a financial deficit, it is
hard to address without implications for teaching and learning at a school as every budget
line must be affected, particularly staffing and resources.
23. In terms of class organisation, the School currently provides 19 classes, with three
for the current reception year of around 22 and 23 pupils each. Other year groups have
some mixed aged classes, as one would expect from a school with a PAN of 75, and some
single year group classes. I note that year 6 has three single year group classes with 20, 22
and 23 pupils. A similar pattern is planned for the 2026/27 academic year for year 6.
24. The School plans 16 classes for the 2026/27 academic year with two classes of 30
for reception year, even though 63 children have accepted places. Sixteen classes are
partly achieved by classes of over 30 pupils in years 3 and 4, which are not infant classes,
and 60 children or fewer in reception year. The School wishes to work towards two classes
to each year group.
25. I note that the local authority forecasts that 68 parents will put the School as their first
preference for 2027/28. Forecasts of the number of children for reception year are
challenging as the children concerned are not in school and forecasts of parental
preference will be largely based on the number of births, the number of children in pre-
5

school provision and previous patterns. It is particularly difficult to forecast demand for
specific primary schools.
26. In considering this matter I have balanced the possible frustration of parental
preference against the likely impact on the School’s financial and educational health of the
PAN remaining at 75. It is probable that if the PAN is 60 in 2027, then a number of parents
may not be able to achieve their first preference. It is clear, however, that there are a high
number of schools within a short distance of the School and so a high chance of admission
to a local school. I note that if the variation is made now, parents will be able to apply in the
knowledge of the PAN set.
27. The number of children seeking a place at the School has fallen, in line with
demographic trends, and the School seeks a pragmatic approach to responding to this with
a PAN which allows it to remain a financially healthy educational establishment. Taking
these matters into account, I approve the reduction in PAN from 75 to 60 for admissions in
2027/28.
28. I also ask the local authority to note that it could request a reduction to the PAN for
2026/27. I cannot say what the outcome of such a request would be and note that any child
for whom a place has been offered would have to be admitted. However, if the PAN were to
be set at 60 and pupil numbers were to reduce to that level, the local authority would not
have to admit over 60 in 2026/27, although it would remain open to any parent refused a
place to appeal.
Determination
29. In accordance with section 88E of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998, I
approve the proposed variation to the admission arrangements determined by Stockport
Metropolitan Borough Council for Broadstone Hall Primary School for 2027/28.
30. I determine that for admission in 2027/28 the published admission number will be 60.
Dated: 14 July 2026

Schools Adjudicator: Deborah Pritchard
